pedagogy.summary: At 6-7, with teacher prompting, the child moves from merely showing a method to EXPLAINING and beginning to JUSTIFY it — using drawings, number sentences, or words to say not just what they did but why the answer is right, including confirming it by an alternative method and spotting an error in a worked example. On the NRICH ladder this spans explaining and convincing. The characteristic gap here is between convincing and justifying: a child at this stage is often confident ('I reckon it's right') with an argument that does not yet hang together as a complete because-chain. Teaching supplies the logical connectives and sentence stems that turn a confident assertion into a reasoned justification, uses alternative-method agreement as a form of justification, and treats error-finding as reasoning practice.
bestPractices: Prompt 'why does that work?' and 'how do you know it's right?' — not just 'what did you do?'
Teach logical connectives and sentence stems ('because', 'so', 'therefore', 'this can't be right because…') to move confident asserting toward complete justification
Use an alternative method that gives the same result as a justification ('the other way also gives 13, so it makes sense')
Use worked examples containing errors and ask children to find and EXPLAIN the mistake
Keep concrete/visual support (drawings, number sentences) as the backbone of the explanation
Distinguish, for yourself and the child, confident-but-incomplete (convincing) from a correct complete chain (justifying), and push gently toward the latter
keyRepresentations: Drawings and number sentences as the medium of explanation
Alternative-method check (two routes to the same answer)
Sentence stems with connectives (because / so / therefore)
The explain → convince → justify steps of the NRICH ladder
commonMisconceptions: Confident assertion ('I reckon it's right') offered as justification, with an incomplete or incoherent chain (convincing mistaken for justifying)
Describing the method but stopping short of saying WHY it gives the right answer unless heavily prompted
Spotting that a worked example is wrong but being unable to explain the flaw
Treating 'justify' as 'do the sum again' rather than giving a reason

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, with adult prompting, children move from showing a method to EXPLAINING and beginning to JUSTIFY it — using drawings, number sentences, or words to say not just what they did but WHY the answer is right. The characteristic gap is between convincing (confident but with an incomplete chain, 'I reckon it's right') and justifying (a correct, complete because-chain). Teaching supplies logical connectives and sentence stems, uses alternative-method agreement as a form of justification, and treats finding and explaining errors in worked examples as reasoning practice.

activities.title: The 'convince me' partner
feedback: When the child only asserts confidently: 'You've convinced me you're sure — now tell me WHY, starting with because…'
When they narrate steps but no reason: 'You made ten first — but why does making ten give the right answer?'
When an alternative method agrees: 'The other way also gives 13, so it makes sense — two routes, same answer.'
When they spot a flawed example only by the odd-looking answer: 'What should have happened at this step? Is each side really the same?'
When they produce a complete chain: name it back so they hear their reasoning hold together.
activities.rationale: Explaining and justifying with prompting is naturally a guided dialogue: a responsive partner can ask 'why does that work?', supply because/so stems, accept an alternative method as evidence, and fold error-critique into the same conversation. Reasoning and its communication develop separately and both benefit from explicit support such as sentence stems and modelling.
sourceClaims: Proficient students justify their conclusions and communicate them, and can distinguish correct reasoning from flawed reasoning and explain what the flaw is; all students can decide whether others' arguments make sense.

Convincing (confident, possibly inaccurate, incomplete chain) is a distinct rung below justifying (a correct, complete chain using because/therefore/so); reasoning and its communication develop separately and both need explicit support (sentence stems, modelling).
learnerActions: Pose the child a within-20 calculation (e.g. 8 + 5) and ask them to explain HOW they worked it out.
Then ask 'why does that work?' and 'how do you know it's right?' — not just 'what did you do?'.
When the child stalls or only asserts ('I just know', 'I reckon it's right'), hand over a sentence stem: 'Start with because…' and prompt for the missing link.
Have the child upgrade a confident hunch into a chain, e.g. 'because 5 is 2 and 3, and 8 and 2 make 10, so 10 and 3 more is 13'.
Ask the child to show the same calculation a different way and check whether it also gives the answer ('the other way also gives 13 — what does that tell us?').
Present a worked example containing a slip (e.g. a number bond that doesn't actually make ten) and ask 'Is this right? How can you tell?' — pushing for WHICH step is wrong and WHY.
activities.intendedInsight: A confident answer is not the same as a justification; a reason that works can be built by linking steps with 'because' and 'so', and an alternative method that agrees is supporting evidence that backs up the reason, though it does not replace explaining why.

activities.title: Build an explanation you can test
feedback: If the chain skips a link: 'Something's missing between here and here — what goes in between, starting with because?'
If the second method disagrees: 'Two routes gave different answers — one of them has a slip; let's find it.'
On a correctly identified and explained error: confirm the step AND the reason, not just the flag.
If the child flags an error without a reason: 'You're right it's wrong — now which step, and what should have happened?'
activities.rationale: Arranging steps and connective words (because/so/therefore) and running an alternative-method or error check can make justification a concrete thing the child constructs and tests, rather than a phrase to recite; the explicit support of sentence stems and modelling is what the research emphasises. Draggable step cards, connective tiles, an 'check it another way' tool and a tap-the-wrong-step error mode are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required.
sourceClaims: Convincing (confident, possibly inaccurate, incomplete chain) is a distinct rung below justifying (a correct, complete chain using because/therefore/so); reasoning and its communication develop separately and both need explicit support (sentence stems, modelling).
learnerActions: Give the child step cards (number sentences / method steps) and connective tiles ('because', 'so', 'therefore') to arrange into an argument chain for why a calculation is right.
Have the child read the assembled chain aloud to check it actually hangs together and establishes the claim.
Check the answer a second way (an alternative method) and compare — do the two routes agree?
In an error-spotting task, give a worked example and have the child point to the wrong step AND say why it is wrong.
Keep drawings and number sentences as the backbone of the explanation throughout.
activities.intendedInsight: Justification is something you assemble and test, not just a confident feeling: steps linked with connectives form a chain; a second method checks whether the answer agrees, and checking each step tests whether the chain really holds.

activities.title: Model a complete because-chain (scaffold)
feedback: After modelling: 'Now you say it for a new sum — start each step with because…'
If the child only copies the words: ask them to explain why one of the steps is needed.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal justified example models a complete because-chain and gives a reference point, but it is a scaffold: while only viewing, the child does not construct their own argument, so it must lead into independent construction.
learnerActions: Show a justified worked example where each step is paired with its 'because' reason, e.g. reveal one step at a time so the child sees what a full chain looks like.
After viewing, ask the child to re-tell the chain in their own words, then produce one for a fresh calculation themselves.
activities.intendedInsight: A worked justification shows the TARGET: every step has a reason, and the reasons connect to establish the answer.

activities.title: Critique items: real reason or just saying it's right? (complement)
feedback: After a choice, ask the child to say WHY the chosen reason is the proper one, so selection leads back to constructing their own explanation.
On the counterexample: 'The answer is right — but does the reasoning always work?'
activities.rationale: Selected-response critique items can probe whether a child recognises flaws and distinguishes reasons from assertions, but a recognition/selected-response format cannot assess a child BUILDING their own justification, so it complements rather than replaces the dialogue and construction activities. No comparative efficacy of this format over others is claimed.
sourceClaims: Proficient students justify their conclusions and communicate them, and can distinguish correct reasoning from flawed reasoning and explain what the flaw is; all students can decide whether others' arguments make sense.
learnerActions: Present short 'find the error' items where the child selects the faulty step in a worked example, then says why it is faulty.
Present 'which is a proper reason vs just saying it's right?' items where the child picks the genuine justification over a confident restatement.
Use an open discussion counterexample (child must explain, not just pick): 'Someone got the right answer with a method that only works because these numbers are small — is their reasoning good?'
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising the difference between a reason and a confident assertion, and between good reasoning and a lucky right answer, may help a child see what a proper justification needs; recognising a good reason does not by itself produce one, so these items complement — not replace — the construction tasks.

constraints: Target the gap between convincing and justifying: confident-but-vague is a normal developmental rung, NOT wrong reasoning — hand over connectives and ask for the missing link rather than marking it wrong.
Do not accept 'do the sum again' or 'because it's right' as justification; the target is a reason WHY the method gives the right answer.
Keep concrete/visual support (drawings, number sentences) as the backbone of explanation at this age.
Modelled/tap-to-reveal justified examples are scaffolds: the child sees a chain but does not build one, so always follow with independent construction.

Selected-response critique items assess recognition of flaws and reasons, not the child's own construction of a justification; use them to complement, not replace, dialogue and building tasks. Recognising a good reason does not by itself elicit producing one.
Error-finding should require naming the faulty step AND why it is faulty, anchored on the meaning of equality (is each side really the same?), not just flagging that the answer looks off.
Alternative-method agreement is used here as a form of justification ('two routes, same answer') — frame it as supporting the reason, not as a substitute for explaining why the method works.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The claim that 'explaining arithmetic reasoning is not spatial' (used to dismiss a 3D format) is a catalog fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law; it has been omitted rather than asserted as universal.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 8 + 5 = 13 via make-ten (8 + 2 = 10, then 10 + 3 = 13) is correct and preserved. The flawed-worked-example task deliberately contains an error for the child to find — ensure any wrong step shown is clearly labelled as the item to critique, not presented as a correct model.

The source claims support the general principles (justifying vs convincing; distinguishing correct from flawed reasoning) but do not establish the comparative efficacy or necessity of any specific format (dialogue, step-card builder, critique items, etc.); efficacy wording is kept qualified (proposed/may/intended).

Independent review confirms activity 4's intended insight and rationale are consistent with the limit that recognition does not elicit production; the embedded counterexample is now explicitly an open explain-why probe, not a scored selection.

probeDeeper: 'Why does making ten first give the right answer — start with because…' (pushes assertion into a reason)
'Show it a different way — does that also give 13? What does that tell us?' (alternative method as justification)
'This worked example is wrong — which step, and why?' (explain a flaw, not just flag it)
Counterexample: 'Someone got the right answer using a method that only works because these numbers are small — is their reasoning good?' (reasoning vs a lucky answer)
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who explains the method AND gives a reason it works ('because 8 and 2 make 10, then 3 more is 13'), uses an alternative method as confirmation, and, shown the flawed example, says it is wrong and points to WHY. A complete because-chain and the ability to explain an error are the targets, not the arithmetic.

errorPatterns.pattern: Convincing mistaken for justifying — confident assertion ('I reckon it's right', 'definitely') with an incomplete or incoherent chain of reasoning.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not treat confident-but-vague as wrong reasoning; hand over connectives ('because… so…') and ask for the missing link. This is a normal rung below justifying and firms up with modelling.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child is sure and fluent but the argument skips steps or does not actually establish the claim; confidence outruns the logic.

errorPatterns.pattern: Describes the method but stops short of WHY it works, unless heavily prompted.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt 'why does making ten work?' and use the alternative-method check ('the other way also gives 13 — what does that tell us?') to surface a reason.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child narrates 'I made ten first' but, asked why that gives the right answer, restates the steps rather than giving a reason.

errorPatterns.pattern: Spots that a worked example is wrong but cannot explain the flaw.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the step and ask 'what should have happened here?'; anchor on the meaning of equality (is each side really the same?) and model naming the flaw.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says 'that's wrong' because the answer looks off, but cannot identify the faulty step or say why it is faulty.

responseLevels.gap: Restates the answer or 'because it's right'; no reason; can flag the flawed example only by the wrong answer, if at all.
responseLevels.full: Gives a complete because/so chain for why the method works, uses an alternative method as genuine confirmation, explains precisely why the worked example is wrong, and does so with only light prompting.
responseLevels.partial: Explains the method and, prompted, is confident it is right and may check another way — but the justification is asserted rather than reasoned (convincing), and the error is spotted without a clear why.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Pose a calculation such as 8 + 5. Ask: 'Explain how you'd work it out — and why is your answer right? Can you show it a different way to check?' Then show a worked example with an error (e.g. a bond that doesn't make ten) and ask: 'Is this right? How do you know?' Discuss the reasoning; do not mark a number.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who justifies produces a connected because/so chain and can say why the error is an error. A child who only convinces asserts confidently ('I reckon it's right') with gaps, and on the flawed example can say 'it's wrong' (answer mismatch) but not name the faulty step. The presence of a complete reasoned chain, and of an explained flaw, is the discriminator.
